Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 4 periods = 160 minutes
Total: 4 periods · 2h 40min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Picture Reading (pp.1–2): observe the four sequenced pictures of the duck, hen, and their young ones.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays Textbook pp.1–2 and invites students to look quietly at all four pictures before any talking begins. Ask: 'What do you notice first?'

Picture Reading — teacher walks students through each illustration in order, pointing to characters, the countryside, and the stream. Students name what they see; teacher reads the speech-bubble dialogue aloud for each picture.
Pairs take turns retelling the picture sequence to each other in one or two spoken sentences per picture, using the illustrations as their prompt.
Whole-class close: teacher asks 'What do you think the duck's plan was?' and takes two or three spoken responses, leaving the question open for students to sit with.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage encounter a wordless-plus-dialogue picture story for the first time in the chapter — linger on each picture so everyone builds the same mental sequence before speaking. The stream crossing is the key dramatic moment; let students speculate about the duck's plan rather than confirming it immediately, as that curiosity sharpens their engagement with the images.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Now discuss with your friends (p.3): guided conversation on the picture story and personal helping experiences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the dialogue text aloud — Duck inviting the hen, the hen's alarm at the stream, the duck's reassurance — so the story is fresh in everyone's mind before discussion begins.

Now discuss with your friends (p.3): teacher poses the first three questions one at a time — counting ducklings and chicks, deciding whether the duck and hen are friends and giving a reason, and explaining how the chicks crossed. Students answer aloud in pairs, then a few pairs share with the class.

Now discuss with your friends (p.3): teacher poses the personal questions — a time a student helped a friend, and whether they felt happy afterwards. Students share briefly with their partner, then two or three share with the whole group.
Class draws together: teacher invites one student to retell the whole story in three spoken sentences using the pictures, then asks the class to add anything the reteller left out.

periods.teacher_notes: Having talked through the picture sequence together, students now bring the story's friendship theme into their own lives — acknowledge all personal helping stories warmly, however small, as this builds the confidence to speak. Watch for students who conflate counting the parents with counting only the young ones in question one; a gentle prompt to look at the pictures again is enough.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Match the following animals with their young ones (p.3): match Duck, Hen, Cow, Cat, Dog to their young.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the five animal names on the board — Duck, Hen, Cow, Cat, Dog — and says each word aloud; students repeat. Teacher then writes the five young-one names in scrambled order and reads them together with the class.

Match the following animals with their young ones (p.3): teacher models one pair aloud ('Duck — the young one is duckling; I know because we saw the ducklings in our story'), then students work individually to draw lines matching each animal to its young one in their textbooks.
Pairs compare their matching and discuss any differences, then the teacher reveals each correct pair on the board one at a time, asking a student to say the pair aloud before confirming it.
Quick oral game: teacher calls out an animal name at random and students call back the young-one name as a class, picking up pace for the final few rounds.

periods.teacher_notes: The pairs duck–duckling and hen–chick are already known from the picture story, so anchor the lesson there before introducing the three new pairs. Students often confuse puppy with kitten at this stage; the oral game at the close gives the teacher a quick read on who has secured the pairings.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Story Together — Voices and Meanings

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Picture Reading (pp.1–2): choral reading of the dialogue across all four pictures.
Now discuss with your friends (p.3): retell the story including the friendship theme and the duck's plan.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the full dialogue text aloud with expression — duck, hen, and narration voices distinct — while students follow in their textbooks on pp.1–2. Students then join in for a second read as a choral group.

Picture Reading (pp.1–2): class is split into two groups — one voices the Duck, one voices the Hen — and they read the dialogue across the four pictures together, with the teacher reading any narration lines.

Now discuss with your friends (p.3): in groups of three, students retell the whole story in their own words — who the friends are, what problem arose at the stream, and how the duck's plan solved it. Each group nominates one person to share their retelling.

Closing reflection: teacher asks the class in one spoken sentence — 'What did you learn from the duck and the hen?' — and takes three or four responses, drawing out the idea that a friend's strength can solve what the other cannot manage alone.

periods.teacher_notes: The choral reading builds on the picture-walk and discussion that explored this story, giving students a chance to inhabit the dialogue with their own voices rather than simply observe it. For the retelling, students who were quiet in earlier discussions often find a small group the safer place to speak — circulate and prompt gently rather than calling on anyone in front of the whole class.

items.source_context: Four sequenced pictures of duck, hen, ducklings, and chicks travelling to a fair and crossing a stream.
items.item_stem: Look at the picture story in your textbook on pages 1 and 2. Why was the hen worried when they reached the stream?

options.label: A
options.text: She could not swim and did not know how to get her chicks across.

options.label: B
options.text: She did not want to go to the village fair.

options.label: C
options.text: She had lost her chicks along the way.

options.label: D
options.text: The stream was too wide for the ducklings to cross.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student has confused a different problem with the hen's actual difficulty at the stream.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a misreading of the story's opening, where the hen agrees eagerly to go to the fair.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows the student has focused on the ducklings rather than the hen's inability to swim as the root problem.

items.source_lo: Student interprets a sequenced visual story and infers meaning using a picture narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four sequenced pictures of duck, hen, ducklings, and chicks travelling to a fair and crossing a stream.
items.item_stem: Look at the picture story on pages 1 and 2. The duck said 'I have a plan.' What do you think the duck's plan was, and how did it help the hen's chicks? Write two sentences.

expected_elements: Duck's plan involved the ducklings helping.
Chicks rode on ducklings' backs across stream.
All animals crossed safely to the other side.

items.source_lo: Student discusses observations, explains reasoning, and retells a story orally using a guided-conversation and retelling mode as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Duck and hen's friendship, the stream-crossing problem, and personal helping experiences from the story.
items.item_stem: Look at the pictures on pages 1 and 2. How can you tell that the duck and the hen are good friends? Give one reason from the story.

options.text: The duck invites the hen to go to the village fair together.
The duck makes a plan to help the hen's chicks cross the stream.
The hen leaves her chicks behind so she can cross the stream alone.
The hen swims across the stream to show she is a good friend.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statements 1 and 3 are true. The duck invites the hen to the fair, showing she wants to share a good time; and the duck uses her swimming ability to help the hen's chicks cross, showing she looks out for her friend's difficulty.

items.item_stem: Tell your teacher or a partner: retell the whole story of the duck and the hen in your own words. Include where they were going, the problem they faced, and how they solved it.

expected_elements: Names the destination — the village fair.
States the problem — hen cannot swim.
Explains the solution — ducklings carried chicks.
